role: Founder of Japanese Sōtō Zen; author of the Shōbōgenzō. Coiner and radical re-reader of Buddhist vocabulary.
Late Song Caodong master at Tiantong Mountain; Dōgen's Chinese teacher. Source of several formulations Dōgen later naturalized into Sōtō vocabulary.
Tang Chan master in the Caodong proto-lineage. Source of dialogues Dōgen later wove into Sōtō practice vocabulary (notably 非思量 in the Fukanzazengi).
Founder of the Caodong (Sōtō) lineage. Coiner of the Five Ranks (五位) and other dialectical formulations central to the school's doctrinal vocabulary.
Dongshan's principal heir; co-namesake of the Caodong lineage. Systematized the Five Ranks doctrinal apparatus.
Tang Chan master in the Guishan-Yangshan circle-figure tradition. Source of the 円相 (ensō) teaching device later naturalized into Japanese Zen calligraphy.
Edo-period Rinzai reformer; systematizer of the modern Rinzai koan curriculum. Reintegrated Caodong-origin vocabulary back into Rinzai training.
Edo-period Rinzai master at Shōfuku-ji; calligrapher-painter whose ensō and Zen brushwork carried the visual-doctrinal vocabulary into the modern period.
Edo rangaku physician; lead translator of the Kaitai Shinsho (1774). Coiner of anatomical and physiological vocabulary including 神経 (nerve).
Bakumatsu rangaku chemist and botanist. Coiner of foundational chemical vocabulary (酸素, 水素, 窒素, 細胞) in the Seimi Kaisō (1837) and Shokugaku Keigen (1834).
Bakumatsu rangaku chemist. Coined 化学 (c. 1860), replacing the earlier phonetic loan 舎密 (seimi).
Late-Edo geographer. Introduced 共和 as the Japanese rendering of "republic" in his Kon'yo Zushiki (1845–46), repurposing the classical Chinese Zhou-dynasty regency reference.

Meiji liberal intellectual and educator; founder of Keiō. Through Seiyō Jijō (1866–70), Bunmeiron no Gairyaku (1875), and Gakumon no Susume, shaped or popularized much of the liberal-political and civilizational vocabulary cluster (自由, 民主, 文明).
The most systematic Meiji coiner of philosophical vocabulary. Coined 哲学, 概念, 主観/客観, 帰納/演繹, 心理学, and many others. Studied in the Netherlands; his coinages reflect Dutch and German engagement.
Meiroku-sha founding member; legal translator. Worked alongside Nishi Amane on the early constitutional and legal-translation vocabulary.
Meiji legal translator. Rendered the Napoleonic codes into Japanese (1870–74) and Wheaton's Elements of International Law (1865), coining or stabilizing much of the modern Japanese legal vocabulary.
Early-Meiji science educator. Author of Butsuri Kaitei (物理階梯, 1872), which fixed 物理 (physics) in the school curriculum.
Meiji liberal political thinker and translator of Rousseau. Coined 美学 (aesthetics) through his 維氏美学 (1883–84), translating Eugène Véron's L'Esthétique.
Founder of the Meiji public-health administration. Re-coined 衛生 (c. 1872–75) from the Zhuangzi's 衛生之經 to translate the German administrative field of Gesundheitspflege / Hygiene.
Principal architect of the Meiji Constitution (1889) and its authoritative gloss (憲法義解). Institutionalized 憲法 and the broader constitutional-political vocabulary.

Leader of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動). Co-author of the 1874 Petition for the Establishment of a Popularly Elected Assembly (民撰議院設立建白書), which circulated 国会 into the political lexicon.

Chinese reform intellectual; the principal return-flow agent. After years in Japan, brought the wasei-kango political and philosophical vocabulary systematically back into Chinese discourse through Xinmin Shuo (1902–06) and other works.
Meiji zoologist; translator of E. S. Morse's 1877 evolution lectures into 動物進化論 (1883). Popularized 進化 (evolution) and the surrounding biological vocabulary.
Meiji academic philosopher. Lead editor of the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881; expanded 1884, 1912) — the lexicon that stabilized the standard Meiji renderings for Western philosophical vocabulary.
Meiji jurist and academic philosopher. Co-editor of the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and a stabilizer of Meiji philosophical and legal vocabulary.
